title: Lebanon’s Imperiled Transition: The Need for an Urgent Reset
gist: Paul Salem argues Lebanon's post-2025 transition has stalled near its two-year mark—no IMF deal, fitful disarmament of Hezbollah, minimal gains from Israel talks—because the president, PM, and Speaker Berri are misaligned; he proposes a three-month emergency rescue plan launched on Nov 22 with IMF legislation by February 2027.

insights.claim: Lebanon's new leadership took office in 2025 promising to restore sovereignty after years of Syrian and Iranian domination, rebuild institutions, and address the economic and banking collapse that began in 2019, aided by shifts in Syria and in Hezbollah's strategic position.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Lebanon's recovery story hinges on whether the post-Hezbollah regional opening can be converted into reforms.
insights.locator: Lebanon’s new leadership came into office

insights.claim: The Lebanese Armed Forces began expanding state authority in the south with a phased deployment plan, but renewed war interrupted implementation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Security normalization in south Lebanon is reversible and exposed to regional conflict.

insights.claim: Lebanon's government took significant decisions on Hezbollah's military activities and Iranian military personnel, filled long-vacant posts, repaired ties with Arab states and the US, and entered direct negotiations with Israel—described as a bold initiative.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Direct Lebanon-Israel talks are a notable diplomatic shift with implications for regional risk premia.
insights.quote: The decision to enter direct negotiations with Israel was a bold initiative

insights.claim: Near the two-year mark of the new mandate, progress toward sovereignty and reform appears dangerously stalled: the state's monopoly on force is fitful with no clear horizon, and banking restructuring and an IMF-supported recovery remain unresolved.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: No IMF program means continued depositor losses and frozen Lebanese sovereign debt restructuring; Eurobond recovery thesis remains delayed.
insights.quote: progress toward real sovereignty and fundamental reform appears dangerously stalled
insights.locator: Yet, as we approach the two-year mark

insights.claim: Negotiations with Israel have reduced attacks on Beirut, but escalation and occupation in the south continue; the first agreed pilot zones covered only three small villages and no new ones have been agreed.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The tiny pilot-zone footprint is a concrete gauge of how little security progress has occurred.
insights.quote: the first pilot zones agreed upon included only three small villages, and no progress has been made to agree on new ones
insights.locator: Yet, as we approach the two-year mark

insights.claim: Paul Salem judges renewed regional conflict to be dangerously likely, and warns it could include Lebanon and undo the limited gains made so far.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Regional escalation risk (Iran-Israel-Hezbollah) remains elevated; relevant to Levant and oil risk premia.
insights.quote: renewed regional conflict—which appears dangerously likely—could include Lebanon
insights.locator: Yet, as we approach the two-year mark

insights.claim: The obstacles are entrenched interests—armed and unarmed—and a hard external environment, but the absence of a coordinated national strategy has made them harder to overcome.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Execution risk is political coordination, not just capacity—watch for a unified elite plan.
insights.quote: the absence of a coordinated national strategy has made these obstacles harder to overcome
insights.locator: Yet, as we approach the two-year mark

insights.claim: Lebanon's three principal state players—the president, the prime minister, and the parliament speaker—are not fully aligned on restoring the state's monopoly over force or on the financial reforms needed for an IMF-supported recovery.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Misalignment at the top is the key bottleneck to an IMF deal; a coordinated plan would be a positive catalyst.
insights.locator: A key challenge is that the three

insights.claim: The president and prime minister rose on public support for change but relied on state insiders to deliver it instead of mobilizing that support; incumbent parties, interest groups, and 'deep-state denizens' resist change.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Without public mobilization, status-quo forces are expected to win, implying reform delays persist.
insights.quote: without which the established forces of the status quo will win out
insights.locator: Part of the challenge is that the president

insights.claim: Speaker Nabih Berri, leader of Amal and of the devastated Shiite community, must choose between the status quo of Iran's IRGC and Hezbollah dragging Lebanon into repeated wars and joining state-building; Salem says he keeps putting off difficult decisions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Berri's stance is a pivotal swing variable for legislation on disarmament and banking reform.
insights.quote: he seems to continue to put off difficult decisions, even as the south and his community spiral deeper into ruin

insights.claim: Many Lebanese still cannot recover their bank deposits, public services remain inadequate, and accountability for the financial collapse and the Beirut port explosion remains incomplete, risking further erosion of public confidence.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Unresolved deposit losses remain the core of Lebanon's banking crisis and a political flashpoint.
insights.quote: Many Lebanese people remain unable to recover their deposits

insights.claim: Despite support from the United States, Europe, and the Gulf states, international skepticism is mounting that Lebanon's leadership can achieve sovereignty and reform.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Donor fatigue could reduce reconstruction financing and investment flows.
insights.quote: there is mounting skepticism and dismay

insights.claim: A failed transition would return Lebanon to a corrupt state without real sovereignty, a pattern that suits nonstate and illicit financial actors and that Iran and Israel might also find convenient.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Some powerful external actors may not want a strong Lebanese state—reform tailwinds are weaker than they appear.
insights.quote: That pattern suits nonstate and illicit financial actors just fine, and some regional actors, including Iran and Israel, might also find it convenient.

insights.claim: Salem proposes the president use the November 22 Independence Day address to launch a three-month emergency initiative with the prime minister, cabinet, parliament, and speaker to agree a time-bound national rescue and recovery plan with security, economic, and diplomatic components, without extraconstitutional mechanisms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Nov 22 address is a near-term signal to watch for whether Lebanon re-commits to reform.

insights.claim: The proposed plan calls for the banking, fiscal, and financial legislation required for an IMF agreement to be adopted by February 2027.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: February 2027 is a benchmark date for any Lebanon IMF deal and related debt restructuring.
insights.quote: with the necessary legislation adopted by February 2027

insights.claim: Salem urges consolidating state authority in the pilot zones and a phased, geographically sequenced plan for a state monopoly on arms extending beyond the south, starting with Beirut, with clear benchmarks and timelines.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Disarmament sequencing beginning in Beirut would be a major test of Hezbollah's residual power.

insights.claim: Delivering reforms would strengthen Lebanon's hand to work with the US toward a full Israeli withdrawal and attract support for the Lebanese Armed Forces, Internal Security Forces, border control, intelligence, infrastructure reconstruction, and private investment.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reconstruction and private investment opportunities are conditional on reform delivery first.
